newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Hong Kong to change with pension rules.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Hong Kong to change with pension rules.

text.p: The Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) promises to become a key pillar of Hong Kong's financial infrastructure, but its greatest influence will weigh on the British colony's funds industry.
Notorious for their lack of enthusiasm for unit trusts, working Hong Kong people could soon be required to contribute 10 percent of their monthly salaries to approved retirement funds.
The consequences are expected to change Hong Kong's investment landscape dramatically, partly by encouraging people to think more about saving for the future.

"If you point to the average Hong Kong citizen and ask them what their pension plan is, they point to their children," said Mike Ryder-Richardson, director of marketing with Jardine Fleming Unit Trusts.
"That is changing. The demographics are changing, with the population aging and changing culturally. People are seeing the need to provide for themselves," he said.

At the moment, Hong Kong's funds industry is dominated by foreign institutional funds dedicated to Asian investment. These funds accounted for about 70 percent of an estimated US$94 billion under management, according to a recent Investment Funds Association survey.
But the MPF could contribute US$5 billion annually into a fund that is expected to top US$150 billion by 2015.

This is expected to add considerable liquidity to the Hong Kong stock exchange while lighting a fire under the territory's dormant debt market as investors seek low-risk, long-term investments with stable yields.
But considerable uncertainty still hangs over the MPF.
Hong Kong's Legislative Council has passed framework legislation allowing its creation, but subsidiary legislation and regulations are still being drafted -- and that is taking longer than expected.

A spokeswoman at the MPF office in Hong Kong said on Friday that the regulations should be ready by April, which leaves just a few months for the legislation to be enacted before the British colony returns to Chinese rule on July 1.
"It's not too much time, but we are working very hard on this," said Maureen To, assistant director at the MPF office.
The question remains whether China will want to support the plan, which forms a cornerstone of Hong Kong's controversial social reform package.
Desmond Chan, who sits on the Hong Kong Investment Funds Association's pension sub-committee, is convinced the MPF will meet little resistance.

"The MPF can kill two birds with one stone," said Chan. "Old age is a very big problem for Hong Kong -- people are getting older. Secondly, the MPF can help to reinforce Hong Kong's financial position in the region."
Chan also said China was rarely reluctant to reveal its disapproval of policy initiatives, which suggests that its silence on the issue is golden.
"If the Chinese side doesn't like an arrangement, they come out and speak quickly," he said. "I don't see why the Chinese side would not support it."
